stem:
A 62-year-old man with chronic heart failure and an ejection fraction of 30% is started on lisinopril. At a follow-up visit two weeks later he reports mild fatigue but no angioedema. Repeat electrolytes show a serum concentration of 5.6 mEq/L, up from 4.1 mEq/L at baseline.

Reduced activity of which of the following collecting-duct processes most directly explains the new hyperkalemia?

options.label: A
options.text: ADH-dependent insertion of apical aquaporin channels
options.misconception: A water-permeability step is being blamed for a potassium change.
options.explanation: Aquaporin insertion controls water recovery, not potassium secretion; ACE inhibition lowers angiotensin II and aldosterone, which reduces principal-cell Na+/K+ exchange.

options.label: B
options.text: Aldosterone-driven principal-cell sodium recovery and potassium secretion
options.misconception: None; less aldosterone means less principal-cell K+ secretion into the urine.
options.explanation: ACE blockade reduces angiotensin II formation and thereby aldosterone; aldosterone normally stimulates principal cells to recover Na+ and secrete K+, so its fall raises serum potassium.

options.label: C
options.text: Intercalated-cell apical proton secretion into the tubular lumen
options.misconception: Acid handling is being substituted for potassium handling.
options.explanation: Intercalated cells secrete H+; the ACE-inhibitor hyperkalemia reflects reduced aldosterone-driven K+ secretion by principal cells.

options.label: D
options.text: Macula densa sensing of tubular sodium chloride delivery
options.misconception: The afferent sensing step is being treated as the effector that moves potassium.
options.explanation: Macula densa signaling modulates renin release; the proximate cause of the potassium rise is reduced aldosterone action on principal cells.

options.label: E
options.text: Proximal-tubule bulk reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate
options.misconception: A proximal acid–base process is being cast as the potassium effector.
options.explanation: Proximal bicarbonate recovery is not the ACE-inhibitor potassium mechanism; principal-cell aldosterone-dependent K+ secretion is.

context: Learning objective: link ACE inhibition to hyperkalemia via aldosterone. Less ACE → less angiotensin II → less aldosterone → less principal-cell Na+ recovery / K+ secretion → higher serum K+.
